un-ga-res-a-69-34:
Mines buried in fields and roads kill and maim long after wars end. Resolution A/69/34, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, renews the long fight against anti-personnel mines. Such mines kill or wound thousands each year, women, girls, boys, and men. They put whole towns at risk and hold back the growth of the lands where they lie.

The Assembly states its will to end that suffering in full. States must do their utmost, in joint and well-steered work, to clear the mines sown across the world and to see them destroyed. Care and healing for the hurt, and help to fit them back into daily life, stand as part of the same duty.

William Gemmell's translation presents the Diamond Sutra, a short Mahayana Buddhist scripture cast as instruction from the Buddha to his disciple Subhuti. Its central teaching is emptiness: all things lack a fixed, separate self. Even Buddhist concepts must not be clung to as final possessions.

Images make the point vivid. Phenomena are like stars at dawn, a bubble in a stream, a flash of lightning, or a dream. The sutra's fame also rests on its copies: a printed version dated 868 AD ranks among the world's oldest surviving printed books. Readers get a demanding text in brief compass, built to cut attachment.
tob-9334:
Early Christians passed down a short manual called the Didache, or Teaching of the Twelve Apostles. Philotheos Bryennios edited the text after finding its only full copy in 1873, ending a loss that had lasted about a thousand years. Scholars date the manual to the church's first generations.

In a few brief chapters it tells believers how to baptize, how to fast and pray, and how to share the Eucharist meal. It also warns how to test traveling prophets and spot false ones. No other text shows so plainly how the earliest churches ran their common life, day by day.
tob-4185-78134:
Goodwin's edition of Plutarch's Moralia opens with volume one, devoted largely to essays on character and conduct. Plutarch writes as a practical counselor. He tells readers how to master anger, check curiosity about others, and find calm of mind amid trouble.

Other pieces advise on education, health, and listening well to lectures. The tone is friendly, the examples drawn from Greek and Roman history. English readers who knew only the Lives met a different Plutarch here: a philosopher of daily life. Goodwin's complete Victorian translation of the essays begins with this humane, useful volume.
tob-4134:
Isaac Myer's Qabbalah, published in 1888, joined two subjects: the philosophy of Solomon ibn Gebirol and the roots of Jewish Kabbalah. Gebirol, an eleventh-century Spanish Jewish thinker, wrote the Fountain of Life, a Neoplatonic account of matter, form, and the divine will. Myer prints and explains his system.

Around it he builds one of the first American studies of Kabbalah's sources and growth. The book opened Jewish philosophy to English readers who had no other road in. Verified from the 1919 edition, Myer's work is dated in spots, yet its pioneering scope still earns respect from historians of mysticism.
tob-10034:
Virgil wrote the Georgics as a poem about farming in four books, at the height of his powers. Mackail's translation is the version named for this entry. It treats the land as serious work fit for great verse.

Book one covers crops and weather signs, book two vines and trees, book three cattle and horses, and book four bees. Virgil mixes plain farming advice with myth, praise of country life, and dark notes on plague and loss. Farmers, poets, and rulers read it for centuries, and it remains the finest farming poem in Latin.
basile-pentamerone-1634:
Giambattista Basile, a courtier of Naples, wrote these tales in the tongue of his town in 1634 to 1636. John Edward Taylor turned them into English in 1850. The set is the first great hoard of fairy tales in Europe, made before Perrault or the Grimms.

Frame tales hold fifty tales told over five days, in a rich, sly style. Sea tales stand among them, such as the Dolphin bridegroom who weds a king's child. The book is the spring from which much of the fairy tale art of Europe first flowed. Its dialect tales keep a snap and color no smooth text could hold.
sale-koran-1734:
George Sale, an English lawyer with a fine grasp of Arabic, made this English Koran in 1734. It was the first English form made straight from the Arabic text. With it stands his Preliminary Discourse, a long first word on the faith of Islam and its Prophet.

Sale's text held the field for a hundred years as the Koran of the English world. His notes draw on the best Arabic sources of his day, with care and calm. The pair of text and first word shaped how the West saw Islam for a long age.
pushkin-queen-of-spades-1834:
Alexander Pushkin wrote The Queen of Spades in 1834. It is a short tale of greed, cards, and a ghost. Hermann is a young German officer in St. Petersburg. He hears of an old countess who knows a sure run of three cards.

He forces his way to her rooms at night and scares her to death in his plea. Her ghost then gives him the three cards, with a price on the gift. At the faro table the last card turns to the queen of spades. The tale is the crown piece of Russian tales of the strange.
milton-comus-1634:
John Milton's masque Comus was first performed in 1634 at Ludlow Castle. This volume joins it with L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas. Together they form the classic set of Milton's essential early poems in English and Latin.

Comus, a tempter with a magic cup, traps a lost Lady in his wood. Her brothers and a guardian spirit free her through chastity's strength. L'Allegro praises mirth, and Il Penseroso praises sober thought and study. Lycidas mourns a drowned friend in some of the finest pastoral verse in English. The set shows a young poet of rare range and control.
marcus-aurelius-meditations-casaubon-163:
Marcus Aurelius wrote his Meditations in Greek, and Meric Casaubon made the first English version in 1634. Casaubon gave England the Roman emperor's notebook, not meant for any eyes but his own. He wrote on campaign along the Danube, in Greek, amid war and plague years there.

The notes urge calm, duty, and scorn for fame, wealth, and the fear of death. All is flux, he reminds himself, and the mind can stay free in any fort. He thanks gods and kin, and checks his temper toward fools and flatterers at court. Stoic counsel here is plain, brief, and meant for daily use in hard times. Casaubon's version made the book a fixture of English moral reading for centuries.
rumi-mathnawi-vol-6-nicholson-1934:
Reynold A. Nicholson translated Rumi's Mathnawi, and this sixth volume came out in 1934 in London. The E. J. W. Gibb Memorial volume gives Books Five and Six in Nicholson's landmark English version. It completes the library's Mathnawi set, the fruit of Nicholson's life work on Rumi's great poem.

Jalalu'ddin Rumi's Mathnawi, a vast Persian poem of the 1200s, teaches Sufi faith through tale and discourse. Kings, fools, lovers, and animals act out lessons on love, pride, prayer, and the soul's return. Nicholson's prose, with its notes, aims at sense and order over the music of the Persian original. Book Six breaks off with Rumi's death, its last tale left, fittingly, without an end in time. Scholars still start with Nicholson when they approach Rumi's ocean of stories in English.
carlyle-sartor-resartus-1834:
Thomas Carlyle published Sartor Resartus in book form in the 1830s, a strange and influential work. Its title means the tailor retailored in Latin. An English editor presents the philosophy of clothes of a German professor, Teufelsdrockh. Clothes stand for all outer forms: institutions, customs, and creeds that spirit wears.

The professor's life story mixes comedy, despair, and conversion to affirmation of life. Carlyle pours German idealism into English letters through this fiction. The Everlasting No and the Everlasting Yea name its dark and bright poles. Victorian readers took it as sage philosophy. It remains Carlyle's most original book.
bancroft-history-us-vol-1-1834:
George Bancroft published Volume 1 of his History of the United States in 1834. Bancroft is often called the father of American history. This volume covers the colonial era, from first voyages to the eve of revolution. He treats settlement, charters, wars with France, and the growth of self-rule.

Bancroft writes American history as the advance of liberty under Providence. His research in European archives set a new standard at home. The prose is grand and patriotic in the manner of his age. Later historians revised many judgments, yet honor his pioneering labor. The History grew to ten volumes across forty years. Volume 1 opens that life's work.
howe-mormonism-unvailed-1834:
Eber Dudley Howe was an Ohio newspaper editor who published Mormonism Unvailed in 1834, the first book-length attack on the new faith. Joseph Smith had published the Book of Mormon only four years earlier, and converts were gathering fast. Howe set out to stop the movement with print.

The book gathers sworn statements from Smith's neighbors calling him a fraud and a money-digger. Its famous claim, the Spalding theory, holds that the Book of Mormon was copied from a lost novel by Solomon Spalding. Howe's attack set the terms of anti-Mormon writing for the rest of the century.
pare-workes-1634:
Ambroise Paré was a French barber-surgeon who treated wounded soldiers on sixteenth-century battlefields. He wrote his surgical works in French from hard experience rather than university training. Thomas Johnson translated the full set into English, and the combined volume appeared in London in 1634.

Paré explains how to treat gunshot wounds with gentle dressings instead of boiling oil. He also describes tying off arteries during amputation, making artificial limbs and eyes, and helping women in childbirth. His clear, case-based writing helped turn surgery into a respected craft. The book is a landmark in the birth of modern surgery.
pope-essay-on-man-1734:
Alexander Pope published An Essay on Man in parts during 1733 and 1734, without his name at first. He addressed it to his friend Henry St. John, Lord Bolingbroke, whose ideas shaped its argument. The poem aims at nothing less than a system of the moral universe.

Across four letters, Pope argues that the world forms one great chain of being, with man in the middle. Human pride, passion, and self-love all serve purposes we only partly see. Whatever is, is right became its most quoted and most argued-over line. The essay sums up Enlightenment optimism in polished heroic couplets of remarkable force and balance.
bayle-dictionary-historical-critical-vol:
Pierre Bayle, a French thinker exiled in Rotterdam, published his Dictionnaire historique et critique in 1697. Volume one here opens the second English edition of 1734, The Dictionary Historical and Critical. The work looks like a reference book of lives and facts, article by article, and its vast footnotes carry the real action.

In those notes, called remarks, Bayle weighs evidence, exposes fables, and quietly saws at dogma. Kings, heretics, philosophers, and obscure scholars all pass under his cool, exact gaze. Bayle's Dictionary reaches volume three in the second English edition of 1734. Pierre Bayle built the work at Rotterdam, where he had fled from persecution in France. The French Dictionnaire historique et critique of 1697 became, in English dress, a five-volume monument of learning and doubt.

laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-3:
Planetary motions and lunar theory fill books six and seven of Laplace's Mecanique Celeste. Nathaniel Bowditch published his translation of that third volume in 1834. The Moon's path posed some of the hardest problems in all astronomy. Sailors and navies needed exact lunar tables for finding position at sea.

Laplace attacks the Moon's many small wobbles with powerful analysis. Bowditch adds commentary and tables that make the work usable. The volume stands third in his four volume English set. It shows theory serving a plain practical need. Few books join deep math to sea travel so directly. Its tables guided real ships.
laennec-auscultation-forbes-1834:
Rene Laennec invented the stethoscope and described its use in his French treatise of 1819. John Forbes translated that work into English, and the edition here dates to 1834. Laennec called his method mediate auscultation, meaning listening through an instrument. The stethoscope let doctors hear the chest with new precision.

Laennec links each sound in the chest to a state of the lungs or heart. Breathing, voice, and cough all become signs a doctor can read. His system founded modern diagnosis of chest disease. English speaking medicine learned the method largely from Forbes's version. The book changed what a doctor does at a bedside. Its plates and terms shaped practice.
audubon-ornithological-biography-vol2-18:
Volume two of Audubon's Ornithological Biography came out in 1834, three years after the first. The set forms the text companion to The Birds of America, his giant picture work. Audubon continues his species accounts in the same rich manner. Each bird receives its habits, haunts, food, and breeding ways.

Field notes gathered on long American journeys supply the facts. Tales of travel and hunting sit beside careful watching, as before. Audubon's voice stays vivid, proud, and exact about what he saw. The second volume holds its place in a five volume run. Bird lovers still read these accounts for their freshness. They preserve a wilder America in words.
plos-pone-0003434:

The virus was found lingering in the light zone of germinal centres. Those are training sites inside lymph nodes where immune cells mature. A refuge there could shield the virus from full clearance. Knowing the hiding place helps explain lasting infection in herds. Foot-and-mouth outbreaks close borders to livestock trade within days of first detection.
plos-pone-0003534:
Douglas B. Stairs and co-authors studied a lining change that precedes cancer in this 2008 paper. In Barrett's esophagus, the normal flat lining of the food pipe changes type. It becomes a simple columnar lining, more like the small intestine. That switch is a premalignant step toward cancer.

Two genes, Cdx1 and c-Myc, fostered the start of that change. Their activity helps drive the transdifferentiation program. Naming the initiators shows where the identity switch begins. Blocking that start might halt the march toward cancer. Acid reflux is the usual driver behind this lining change over years.
plos-pone-0003634:
Thomas Widmann, Urban Sester, Barbara C. Gärtner, and colleagues published this transplant study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cytomegalovirus, or CMV, is the most common viral problem after stem cell transplants from donors. The team tracked the T cells that target CMV in patients after transplant.

Levels of these CMV-specific CD4 T cells rose and fell over time in each patient. Their levels tracked closely with how much virus was active in the blood. The pattern suggests that watching these cells could help doctors judge a patient's risk and time treatment against the virus.
plos-pone-0003734:
Yusuke T. Maeda, Junya Inose, Miki Y. Matsuo, and colleagues published this cell movement study in PLOS ONE in 2008. With no signal to follow, most moving cells still crawl by coordinating their own shape changes with their motion. How cells run that coordination on their own was little known.

The authors measured cell shape during spontaneous migration and found ordered patterns. A cell's deformation and its direction of travel stayed correlated in set ways. The study reveals an inner choreography behind the seemingly aimless crawl of cells left to themselves.
plos-pone-0003834:
Neelam Engineer, Keelin O'Donoghue, Ruwan C. Wimalasundera, and colleagues published this pregnancy study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In monochorionic twin pregnancies, too much amniotic fluid, called polyhydramnios, can complicate care. A short cervix raises the risk of early birth. The team tested how the two problems relate.

In a controlled intervention study of forty women, they tracked cervical length as fluid volume was normalized. Their hypothesis was that shortening reflects the degree of excess fluid. The results clarify when extra fluid truly threatens preterm birth in these complicated twin pregnancies.
plos-pone-0003934:
Kleber S. Vieira, Cristina Arzabe, Malva I. M. Hernández, and co-authors measured body variation in a Brazilian toad in 2008. The toad Proceratophrys cristiceps lives only in South America. It inhabits the dry Caatinga region of northeastern Brazil. Little detailed measurement of its body form had been published.

Their PLOS ONE article examines how size and shape vary within one population. Such data show how much a species can differ across a harsh, dry home. The measures help separate this species from close relatives. They also give a base for tracking change as the Caatinga climate shifts.
plos-pone-0004034:
Xiangyang Xue, Jun Sun, Qingfeng Zhang, and co-authors found new microRNAs in a parasitic worm in 2008. Schistosomiasis japonica remains a major public health problem in China. Its worm, Schistosoma japonicum, has a complex life cycle. Genes switch on and off across its life stages.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies and describes novel microRNAs from the worm. MicroRNAs are small regulators that tune gene activity. Stage-specific regulators are promising targets for control. Cataloguing them is a first step toward drugs or vaccines. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004134:
Chihiro Kakiuchi and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Valproate is a standard drug for bipolar disorder and a first-line mood stabiliser, yet how it works in the brain is still unclear. One clue is that it changes gene activity. It also switches on proteins that help cells handle stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, a cell compartment where proteins are folded.

The team reports that valproate raises production of WFS1, a gene also known from a rare form of diabetes. They also show it changes how WFS1 interacts with GRP94, a protein tied to that same stress system. The findings offer one concrete path by which the drug may calm mood swings.
plos-pone-0004234:
Yujun Liang, Shicui Zhang, and Zhiping Wang published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most invertebrates fertilise their eggs externally, so their embryos develop in water full of microbes, many of them dangerous. How those embryos defend themselves was an open question.

Working with amphioxus, a small fish-like animal, the team studied the fluid inside its eggs. They found alternative complement activity there, a part of the innate immune system, and present evidence for a defence role of maternal complement components. In short, the mother loads the egg with weapons before it ever hatches.
plos-pone-0004334:
Ana Mingorance-Le Meur, Alma Mohebiany, and Timothy O'Connor published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The rat PC12 cell line is a traditional model for neurite outgrowth and growth cone behaviour, used because its cells grow neuron-like fibres. To clarify how far PC12 neurite terminals can be compared with real neuronal growth cones, the team analysed their morphology and protein distribution.

They describe two kinds of terminals: varicones and growth cones. Distinguishing them matters, because experiments using this classic cell line may be reading two different structures as one. PC12 cells come from a rat adrenal tumour, called a pheochromocytoma.
plos-pone-0004434: In 2009, Casalbore, Budoni, and Ricci-Vitiani probed nose-derived stem cells. Tumorigenic potential of olfactory bulb-derived neural stem cells was linked to Akt activation. plos-pone-0004534: In 2009, Magdaleno, Ahn, and Paes tested a proline look-alike against Chagas' parasite. Actions of the proline analogue T4C on Trypanosoma cruzi were charted. The analogue disrupted the parasites' proline use. The finding aids Chagas drug design. The amino acid matters hugely.
plos-pone-0004634: In 2009, Miyagawa, Okita, and Itagaki found a cancer switch silencing key Wnt blockers. EWS/ETS regulated Dickkopf family expression in Ewing tumor cells. The fusion protein dialed the blockers down. The finding maps Ewing biology anew. The signaling is Wnt.
plos-pone-0004734: In 2009, Uzan, Figeac, and Portha mapped a growth factor growing pancreas ducts anew. Mechanisms of KGF signaling in pancreatic duct cell growth and specialization were charted. The factor drove epithelial growth strongly. The study maps regenerative medicine research. The specificity is epithelial.
landor-citation-shakspeare-1834:
Landor invented a legal scene for young William Shakspeare in this playful work of 1834. In his telling, the future playwright stands before Sir Thomas Lucy in September 1582, charged with stealing deer from the knight's park. Witnesses named Euseby Treen, Joseph Carnaby, and Silas Gough support the case, by the title page.

Shakspeare defends himself in dialogue with wit, while the magistrate blusters at him. The piece gives the old Stratford deer-stealing legend a full hearing it never had in real life. Added at the end is a talk between Edmund Spenser and the Earl of Essex on the state of Ireland in 1595.
act-of-supremacy-1534:
Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, during the reign of Henry VIII. The law declared the king to be the supreme head of the Church of England. With that step, England broke in law from the authority of the pope in Rome.

The act grew out of Henry's fight with Rome over ending his first marriage. It gave the crown power over church courts, appointments, and doctrine in England. Later monarchs kept, lost, and regained this title as religion shifted. The statute marks the legal start of the English Reformation, a change that remade English life for generations.
cia-0000007534:
Volume 8, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence came out in winter 1964, amid a deepening war in Vietnam. The issue's named subject is the Soviet high command, the top level of the USSR's armed forces. As always, the journal was written by CIA officers for an internal audience.

Studying the Soviet command meant tracing who led, how orders flowed, and where power sat. Work like this shaped how Washington judged Soviet strength during the Cold War. The declassified issue shows analysts sharing their craft with peers, not briefing the press. It remains useful evidence of the agency's working concerns in 1964.
cia-0000008134:
Egypt's leader Gamal Abdel Nasser looked south, and a January 1964 CIA paper tracked his policy in Black Africa. Nasser sought influence among the new states below the Sahara through aid, radio, and diplomacy. His moves formed part of a wider Arab and Cold War rivalry.

The assessment weighs where Cairo was gaining ground and where its reach met limits. Washington read these contests country by country, watching schools, arms, and broadcasts alike. For modern readers, the paper maps how the Middle East's politics spilled into Africa. It also shows intelligence work following soft power, not just armies.
cia-0000012334:
In February 1962 Helms wrote the Director of Central Intelligence once more on the Penkovsky matter, and the case still commanded the top's attention. By then the colonel had been spying for the West for well over a year. His value had not dimmed; if anything, the year's gathering dangers raised it with every passing month.

The memo belongs to the file's sustained focus on one asset above all others. Summit paper moved both ways, questions down and product up. For readers, this page shows a prized source still at the center of his handlers' world in his final year.
cia-0000013234:
Detention and treatment of American prisoners, in both North and South Vietnam, are surveyed in a CIA paper from January 1971. The survey covers the whole system at once. It takes in the captives' daily lives in the camps. It also records the guards' methods, from rations to punishment, as survivors and sources had reported them over the years of the war.

The paper's calm tone cannot hide the suffering it describes. That calm is part of its value as a record. It formed part of the accounting Washington owed the prisoners' families. For readers, it is the humanitarian record of the system, documented whole.
cia-0000013834:
North Vietnamese and Viet Cong policy toward allied prisoners, and toward defectors, is compared in a CIA paper from November 1966. The paper studies the two systems' doctrine side by side. The north's rules ran through Hanoi's ministries; the south's ran through jungle headquarters. frus-1862-d134:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 25 August 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 134 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d234:
Dated 6 September 1862, Document 234 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William Stuart of the British legation in Washington. It is one of two Seward letters to Stuart under that date in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Early September was the season's diplomatic high tide: invasion in Maryland, mediation talk in Europe, and a British cabinet watching for a reason to act. Seward wrote into that moment with his usual frequency. The pair of letters for 6 September shows the Department pressing its case while the military question hung open. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d334:
Two Dayton reports are dated 14 October 1862, and the first stands as Document 334 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went from William L. Dayton in Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Dayton wrote in the week when the French truce plan was complete and only London's answer was missing. His reports tracked the court's confidence and its fallback plans. For Washington, Paris reporting in mid-October was intelligence of the first order, since France's next step depended on signals Dayton was placed to catch. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d434:
Two days after the Spanish minister's note, on 9 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Gabriel García Tassara. The reply is Document 434 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the annual printed record.

Quick replies kept small disputes from growing, and Seward made a habit of prompt, courteous answers to resident ministers. The Spanish file in Washington covered neutral duties, maritime questions, and the aftershocks of the allied landing in Mexico. In August 1862, with a fresh draft of troops at home, the Union needed its foreign ties steady. The note shows Seward tending one of those ties in person, at the pace the wartime post allowed.
frus-1862-d534:
A second note dated 9 June 1862 passed from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 534 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

The doubling of notes on a single day, repeated across this exchange, reflects how enclosures and separate subjects were handled. Nothing was mixed. Everything was numbered and answered in kind. For the Netherlands, the stakes in Washington were commercial and legal, not military. Van Limburg's steady formal pressure was how a small power defended them. The document completes the densest cluster in the Dutch file, five days of letters that show the State Department's wartime desk work at full stretch.
frus-1862-d634:
The year's closing instruction to Constantinople went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Edward Joy Morris on 18 November 1862. It is Document 634 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November's orders everywhere repeated the Union's refusal of foreign mediation. The instruction to the Ottoman post carried that settled policy to the edge of the system. Morris needed it less as guidance than as record: Washington's position, stated to all its ministers alike, could be quoted anywhere. The letter ends the Turkish file for 1862 on the year's dominant diplomatic note. It was sounded as firmly at Constantinople as at London. Yet the audience there could hardly have mattered less to the outcome.
frus-1863p1-d34:
Charles Francis Adams closed his heavy mail day with this third dispatch of 16 January 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 34 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The run of Adams letters in this volume is the spine of the British file. His reports let Washington know, steamer by steamer, whether Britain leaned toward or away from the South. This letter ends a three-sheet day in mid-January, when the freedom edict's echo was still fresh in London. It is a working piece of a watch that helped keep Britain out of the war.
frus-1863p1-d134:
Charles Francis Adams closed the month with this third dispatch of 27 March 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 134 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of a three-letter day wound up the post's March work. Adams's spring file is dense because the stakes were: warships for the South in British yards, and a British cabinet that trod a fine line. This letter ends the day's set. It is a working piece of the great London run, the part of the volume most read by students of the war.
frus-1863p1-d234:
On 13 July 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 234 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d334:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 10 December 1862. It stands as document 334 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d434:
31 March 1863 is the date on a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d534:
Writing on 26 May 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward in an official letter. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d634:
A 8 October 1863 dispatch from the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams reached Secretary of State William H. Seward. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020234:
Rick S. Mitchell, Brett F. Beitzel, Astrid R. W. Schröder, and co-workers compared where retroviruses insert their DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. Retroviruses copy their genes into the host's genome. The team tracked insertion sites for three of them: ASLV, a bird virus; HIV; and MLV, a mouse virus.

Each virus favors different kinds of spots. HIV leans toward active genes, while the others show their own patterns. Those choices affect both harm and use. An insertion inside a vital gene can cause cancer, a known risk in gene therapy with such viruses. Knowing each virus's taste helps predict that risk and pick safer vectors for treatment.
plos-pbio-0020334:
Amit Dutt, Stefano Canevascini, Erika Fröhli, and their team traced a growth signal in the worm C. elegans in PLOS Biology in 2004. EGF signals help shape the worm's egg-laying organ, the vulva, during development. A protein called ROM-1, from the rhomboid family, helps pass that signal along.

Rhomboid proteins cut other proteins inside cell membranes, freeing signal pieces to act. Showing that ROM-1 shapes EGF spread in a living animal gave the family a clear job in development. That matters beyond worms. Human rhomboids and EGF signals are both tied to cancer and to diseases of the skin and gut, so the worm work offers clean leads.
plos-pone-0000134:
Jaime H. Reina, Teldja N. Azzouz, and Nouria Hernandez published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It introduces Maf1 as a player in the control of human RNA polymerase III. That enzyme copies a small but vital set of genes, including ones for transfer RNA, the adapters used to build proteins.

Cells must tune this copying to their growth state, making more building blocks when times are good. The authors show Maf1 helps regulate that process in human cells. The work connects a conserved control protein to basic cell growth, with relevance for understanding diseases where growth control fails.
plos-pone-0000234:
Seiya Tsujiuchi, Elena Sivan-Loukianova, Daniel F. Eberl, and colleagues published this hearing study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honey bees communicate with waggle dance sounds, vibrations made by dancing bees that tell hive mates where food is. The authors examine how the bee auditory system handles these sounds. They focus on dynamic range compression, the squeezing of loud and quiet into a range the ear can manage.

Bees must hear faint dance sounds amid a noisy hive. Compression helps an ear stay sensitive without being overwhelmed. The paper details how the bee's auditory system achieves it. That adds to the science of hearing in insects and to the study of the waggle dance itself.
plos-pone-0000334:
Jonathan H. Fox, Jibrin A. Kama, Gregory Lieberman, and colleagues published this Huntington's disease paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Copper ions interact with the huntingtin protein whose mutant form causes the disease. The authors study the mechanisms by which copper drives the progression of Huntington's disease.

Metals like copper can push toxic proteins to clump or damage cells. Tracing copper's role suggests ways to slow the disease by managing metal chemistry in the brain. The paper joins a line of research treating Huntington's partly as a problem of protein-metal interaction.
plos-pone-0000434:
Kunihiko Kaneko modeled how gene networks stay steady in a noisy world, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Cells must keep their gene expression stable even though molecules collide at random and mutations keep arising. Kaneko studied the evolution of robustness to both noise and mutation in the dynamics of gene expression.

Robustness is itself a trait that evolution can build. Simulations of this kind test whether networks that survive random jolts also, as a side effect, survive genetic change, and vice versa. That question sits at the heart of evolutionary theory. It may explain why living systems are stable day to day. It may also explain how they still evolve over generations.
plos-pone-0000534:
Ping-Ping Chen and colleagues measured three related genes across lung cancer patients, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes, Cyr61, CTGF, and WISP-1, belong to one family involved in growth and tissue repair. Their expression correlated with clinical features of lung cancer, the measurable traits of each patient's disease.

A gene whose activity tracks stage or outcome can serve as a biomarker, helping doctors judge how a tumor will behave. Three family members measured together give a stronger signal than any one alone. Studies like this screen the genome's output for clinically useful patterns in the world's deadliest cancer.
plos-pone-0000634:
Michael A. Brockhurst asked whether population bottlenecks keep cooperation alive in bacterial biofilms, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. A bottleneck is a crash that leaves few survivors to restart a population. Theory assumes such crashes help social traits persist in microbes. Events like colonizing a new site, or a disturbance, can cause them.

A bottleneck raises relatedness among survivors, since offspring descend from a handful of cells. Relatives gain more from each other's cooperation, so cooperative traits can pay. Brockhurst's title gives his answer: bottlenecks do promote cooperation in biofilms, the layered communities bacteria build on surfaces. The result informs debates about how social life evolves in microbes.
plos-pone-0000734:
Jonatan Blais, Ciro Rico, Cock van Oosterhout and colleagues compared immune genes in cichlid fish from Africa's great lakes. The haplochromine cichlids of Lakes Malawi and Victoria are among the most important study systems in evolutionary biology, famous for rapid speciation. Identifying adaptive divergence between closely related species may reveal the processes that built that diversity.

The team focused on MHC genes, which present invader fragments to the immune system and vary hugely between individuals. Their title reports adaptive divergence in MHC between closely related species living in the same waters. Diverging immune genes in side-by-side species suggests parasites and disease help drive cichlid splitting.
plos-pone-0000834:
Leeanne McGurk, Harris Morrison, Liam P. Keegan and colleagues found a way to see inside an intact adult fruit fly, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The major hindrance is the dark exoskeleton: the fly's cuticle blocks imaging of internal organs. The team beat that obstacle. They describe a method to image the internal organs of adult Drosophila in three dimensions. It works by bleaching and clearing the tissue.

Drosophila is genetics' most powerful insect model, yet adult anatomy was largely read from dissections. Whole-body 3D imaging preserves the spatial relations dissection destroys. Screens for internal defects, in guts, brains, or reproductive organs, become feasible at a scale matching the fly's genetic tools.
plos-pone-0000934:
Ethan Decker, Andrew Kerkhoff and Melanie Moses charted how city sizes are spread across the globe, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cities draw in huge flows of energy and materials. Knowing whether a country has many mid sized cities or one giant one shapes how growth can be managed.

The authors look for the fundamental drivers behind those size patterns. Regular patterns across very different countries hint at shared rules of growth. Finding the rules would help planners predict where pressure will build next. It would also help weigh the costs that giant cities place on the wider environment. The study treats cities as a global system, not isolated cases.
plos-pone-0001034:
Edna Caceda and Tadeusz Kochel compared a modified culture method for catching arboviruses in patient samples, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Arboviruses spread by insects, and patient blood often carries too few virus particles to isolate easily. The pair tested a modified shell vial culture procedure against standard detection.

Their panel covered dengue, yellow fever, Saint Louis encephalitis, West Nile, Ilheus, group C viruses, Oropouche, Mayaro and Venezuelan equine encephalitis. A bench method that catches more of these viruses helps clinics in the Americas name infections that look alike. Naming matters, since these diseases differ in risk and in the response they demand.
plos-pone-0001134:
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an inherited disease that affects muscle and many other systems. Esther Llagostera and co-authors studied one of its common features, insulin resistance, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The disease is caused by an expanded repeat in the DMPK gene, which codes for a protein kinase.

The team examined what DMPK itself does in glucose balance and in how muscle responds to insulin. Separating the kinase's normal job from the damage caused by the repeat helps explain why patients handle sugar poorly. The work points to where in this chain a treatment might intervene.
plos-pone-0001234:
Schizophrenia has a strong genetic component, and one suspect region is 22q11.2, a chromosome segment tied to susceptibility. Ruby Hsu and colleagues examined a candidate gene there, RTN4R, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The gene codes for the Nogo receptor 1, which regulates axon growth and limits regrowth after injury.

Using both human and mouse genetic approaches, the authors evaluate evidence for association between common variants in the gene and schizophrenia. A gene that controls wiring in the brain, sitting in a known risk region, is a strong functional and positional candidate. Their analysis weighs whether it truly contributes to the disease.
plos-pone-0001334:
The C/EBP family of transcription factors includes five genes, two of which are essential for ovarian granulosa cell function. A-Mei Huang and colleagues explored a third family member, Cebpd, in the mouse ovary, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cebpd is switched on by luteinizing hormone in theca and interstitial cells of the ovary.

By expression and functional analysis, the authors conclude that Cebpd, while induced by the hormone, is not essential for mouse ovary function. Genes can be hormone-responsive yet dispensable, because relatives compensate. Sorting essential from incidental family members is basic groundwork for reproductive biology.
plos-pone-0001434:
Guillaume Pézeron and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on embryo growth in zebrafish. A growth factor helper plays a key role in forming the germ layers of the embryo. Its loss causes a one eyed mutant form in fish. The team asked which other genes tune that helper's effect.

They found that lowering a gene called rasl11b eased the one eyed trait. In other words, the second gene acts as a brake on the same path. Pairs like this help map the web that guides early growth. They also show how one fault can be softened by a second change nearby.
plos-pone-0001534:
Ralf Engbert and Antje Nuthmann wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eye jumps during reading. As we read, our eyes jump to land each word near the center of view. Faults in that system spread landing spots wide, with overlap between words. That spread made it hard to tell which word a gaze was truly on.

The pair offer a self consistent way to gauge missed landings from the data itself. A sound gauge cleans up decades of reading data. It lets labs test models of eye control with less noise. Reading science gains a sharper tool for a core measure.
plos-pone-0001634:
Yasuhiro Takeuchi and co-authors studied how a virus gene mixes and matches its parts over time, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The gene is cap, from adeno-associated virus, a small virus often used as a carrier in gene therapy. When two versions of a virus infect the same cell, their genes can swap pieces, a process called recombination, which creates mosaic genes.

The authors looked for signs of such swaps across virus samples and asked what the mosaics mean for the virus. The full text gives the sequence comparisons, the swap points they found, and their view of how common this mixing is. The work matters for gene therapy because the cap gene builds the shell that decides which cells the carrier virus can enter.
plos-pone-0001734:
Nelson K. F. Chen, Jen San Wong, Irene H. C. Kee, and their co-authors corrected diabetes in a large animal model with modified liver cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gene and cell therapies face limits that block wide clinical use. Using diabetes as the test case, the team sought to get around those limits.

They took primary liver cells from the animals themselves, added a nonviral insulin expression vector by electrotransfer outside the body, and returned the cells. The treated cells corrected diabetes and prevented target organ injury, per the paper's title. The full text gives the model, the cell handling, and the glucose results. Avoiding viruses as carriers removes a major safety worry for gene therapy.
plos-pone-0001834:
Létitia Jean and co-authors used an enzyme as a model for amyloid formation in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Clumping into amyloid fibrils is a crucial step in brain diseases such as Alzheimer's. How amyloid builds is set by the chain's own traits and specific side chain contacts, since fibrils from unlike proteins share a like shape.

Their cholinesterase model system probes which parts govern the birth of amyloid. The full text gives the fibril tests and the part contrasts. A tractable model enzyme lets labs test anti amyloid ideas quickly, before moving to the disease proteins.
plos-pone-0001934:
Clara Menendez and co-authors ran a trial on malaria care in pregnancy in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In Africa, pregnant women are urged to sleep under insecticide-treated nets and to take preventive doses of malaria drugs at clinic visits. Whether the two work safely together had not been tested.

The team ran a randomized, placebo-controlled trial with one thousand thirty pregnant women in Mozambique. All got nets through the antenatal clinic; some also got the preventive drug doses, and some got a placebo. The design checks whether the drug adds gain on top of nets without adding harm. Proof here guides care for millions of women.
plos-pone-0002034:
Kurt Reed and co-authors modeled where a dangerous fungus lives in Wisconsin, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Blastomycosis is a lung illness that can kill, caught by breathing in spores of the fungus Blastomyces dermatitidis from the environment. Where that fungus lives was poorly known, in part because its niches are hard to find by sampling.

The team used ecological niche modeling, which maps the conditions at known case sites and projects them across the state. A map of likely habitat guides doctors to suspect the illness sooner and guides field teams to the soils where the fungus hides.
plos-pone-0002134:
Ping Kei Chan and co-authors tested a boundary piece of DNA in the beta-globin gene region, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Beta-globin genes make part of hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. A control region switches these genes on at the right times. One site in it, called 5'HS5, was thought to act as a border between active and quiet DNA.

The team removed that site and watched the shape of the gene region using a method that captures how DNA folds in the cell. The active hub of the locus still formed without it. The result narrows down which parts of the control region truly run the show.
plos-pone-0002234:
Jeongheon Yoon and co-authors followed two gene-silencing proteins through the making of eggs in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Germline stem cells in the fly ovary divide unevenly, keeping one stem cell and producing a cystoblast that goes on to form eggs. They are, in effect, immortal stem cells.

The team shows that two enzymes that tag histones, dSETDB1 and SU(VAR)3-9, act one after the other as these cells differentiate. Orderly tagging of the genome's packing helps switch gene sets as a stem cell becomes a gamete. The sequence adds detail to how stem cells hand their potential down one path only.
plos-pone-0002334:
Anuradha Ratnaparkhi, George Lawless, Felix Schweizer, and co-authors built a fruit fly model of an inherited form of ALS, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. ALS8 is a type of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis caused by a dominant mutation in the protein VAPB, which helps membranes meet inside cells. The gene is conserved across evolution, which makes the fly a fair test bed.

The team put the corresponding mutation into the fly version, dVAP33A, and examined the effects. Their results suggest the mutant protein acts through a dominant negative mechanism, poisoning the normal copy's work. A fly model lets researchers screen genes and drugs for this disease quickly and cheaply.
plos-pone-0002434:
A research team led by Edelweiss reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Evelina Edelweiss, Taras G. Balandin, Julia L. Ivanova, and others. Its subject is barnase as a New Therapeutic Agent Triggering Apoptosis in Human Cancer Cells. RNases are currently studied as non-mutagenic alternatives to the harmful DNA-damaging anticancer drugs commonly used in clinical practice.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002534:
Work from Martí and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Daniel Martí, Gustavo Deco, Maurizio Mattia, and others. Its subject is a Fluctuation-Driven Mechanism for Slow Decision Processes in Reverberant Networks. The spike activity of cells in some cortical areas has been found to be correlated with reaction times.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002634:
Luisa Cironi led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was IGF1 is a common target gene of ewing's sarcoma fusion proteins in mesenchymal progenitor cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Luisa Cironi, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The EWS-FLI-1 fusion protein is associated with 85–90% of Ewing's sarcoma family tumors (ESFT). Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002734:
Claudia Wellbrock led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with oncogenic BRAF regulates melanoma proliferation through the lineage specific factor MITF. The catalog record names Claudia Wellbrock first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The Microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) is an important regulator of cell-type specific functions in melanocytic cells. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002834:
Bekim Sadikovic led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was in vitro analysis of integrated global High-Resolution DNA methylation profiling with genomic imbalance and gene expression in osteosarcoma. Authorship is credited in the record to Bekim Sadikovic and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Genetic and epigenetic changes contribute to deregulation of gene expression and development of human cancer. The summary also notes a further point. Changes in DNA methylation are key epigenetic factors regulating gene expression and genomic stability. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002934:
Giselle Chamberlain, Karina Wright, Antal Rot and co-authors compared chemokine receptors on mouse and human stem cells in 2008. Mesenchymal stem cells are marrow stromal cells that can become bone, cartilage, and other tissues. They are rare in marrow but grow well in culture while keeping their range.

Chemokine receptors guide where such cells travel in the body. The PLOS ONE study found the mouse cells carry a restricted set of working receptors, and compared that set with human cells. The contrast warns against assuming mouse results will match patients in stem cell therapy trials.
plos-pone-0003034:
Thomas Burgold, Fabio Spreafico, Francesca De Santa and co-authors studied the histone demethylase Jmjd3 in 2008. Methyl marks at lysine 4 and 27 of histone H3 track with gene activity and repression. Those patterns are set during development and are thought to lock in lineage-specific gene programs.

Jmjd3 removes the repressive mark at lysine 27. The title reports it is required for neural commitment, the step where stem cells commit to becoming nerve tissue. Published in PLOS ONE, the enzyme is a gatekeeper for one major cell fate decision. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003134:
Lu-Ning Liu, Abdalmohsen T. Elmalk, Thijs J. Aartsma and colleagues study how red algae shed excess light energy in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plants and algae that use sunlight have built many ways to avoid damage under bright light. Red algae and cyanobacteria use large antenna complexes called phycobilisomes to harvest light. Some cyanobacteria use an orange protein in this process as well.

Working at the single molecule level, the team describe light-induced energetic decoupling as a route for energy loss tied to phycobilisomes. Readers see protection from bright light at the scale of single complexes. The work adds detail to how algae keep photosynthesis safe.
plos-pone-0003234:
Antonina Y. Alexandrova, Katya Arnold, Sébastien Schaub and colleagues compare cell flow and adhesions in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The dynamic actin network at the leading edge of the cell is linked to the matrix outside through focal adhesions. At the same time, it undergoes retrograde flow. The flow has different dynamics in two distinct zones. Those zones are the lamellipodium, a fast flow zone, and the area behind it.

The title reports that formation of nascent adhesions triggers the transition from fast to slow flow. Readers see adhesion birth and actin flow as coupled events. Cell migration underlies wound healing and cancer spread, so its mechanics matter widely.
plos-pone-0003334:
Thomas R. Welch and Lisa W. Blystone study complement and kidney disease in mice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The role of circulating complement in host defence and immune disease is well established. Although a number of cells and tissues are capable of synthesizing complement components locally, the importance of such local synthesis in immune disease has been difficult to establish.

The authors report immune complex glomerulonephritis following bone marrow transplantation in C3 deficient mice. Readers see a test that separates blood complement from locally made complement. That distinction matters because blocking complement only in one place might treat disease with fewer risks.
plos-pone-0007434: Sanfilippo syndrome type C is a devastating inherited disorder in which children lose mental abilities because a lysosomal enzyme is missing. This study shows the deeper cause: the faulty protein misfolds, so the cell's quality control destroys it before it can work. Recasting the disease as a folding problem opens the door to therapies that help the protein fold correctly.
plos-pone-0007534: Memory and general thinking ability run in families, and this study traced part of that inheritance to variants in DCLK1, a gene switched on by the brain's memory chemical BDNF. People carrying certain variants scored differently on memory and cognition tests. The link connects a molecular growth signal to the everyday differences in how we think.
plos-pone-0007634: As an embryo's skin forms, its cells must cling together while constantly reshaping. This study shows a trafficking protein called Rab11 keeps the adhesion system supplied in fruit fly embryos, maintaining the Crumbs protein at the cell surface and the junctions between cells. The finding reveals the delivery service behind stable-yet-flexible tissue.
plos-pone-0007734: Tagging proteins with arginine marks them for disposal, and this study deleted the tagging enzyme in the mouse germline. The result was defective sperm production and early embryo death. The experiment shows protein arginylation is indispensable for making the next generation.
plos-pone-0007834: Monkeys weigh the value of calls before choosing. This 2009 study tested how rhesus monkeys incorporate vocalizations into free-choice decisions. By measuring how social sounds shift choices, the work reveals how primate brains blend communication signals with economic decision-making.
plos-pone-0007934: Workout-ready muscles got a molecular switch. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Pogozelski's team showed p38γ MAPK tunes muscle fuel use in mice. Endurance training rewires muscle. The tuning switch was mapped. The switch feeds exercise science.
